computationally designed peptides can form self-assembling materials that exhibit a wide range of lattice morphologies across multiple length scales (1–1000 nm) and that these materials can be controlled by tuning solution assembly conditions.

computationally designed peptides can self-assemble into three distinct types of nanostructured latices that are robust to changes in solution conditions and can be used to engineer materials with micrometer-scale morphology.
we have designed and synthesized peptides that form self-assembling nanomaterials with tunable properties.

the design of self-assembling materials that can be controlled by tuning solution conditions.
the design of nanostructured materials using computational design methods and self-assembly.
the design of self-assembling peptide-based materials with complex, predetermined nanostructures.

computationally designed peptide sequences can be used to engineer a wide variety of self-assembled materials with precise control of nanostructure.
the design of nanostructures from computationally designed peptides is possible and that the design of these structures requires the control of the peptide sequence and solution conditions.
computationally designed peptides can be used as building blocks to produce nanostructured materials with controlled properties.

we have designed peptides that can be used for the assembly of nanostructures with a variety of morphologies.
we have demonstrated a computational method to design peptides that can be used to engineer self-assembling materials with nanoscale structure.
we designed peptides that self-assembled into nanostructures with the designed morphology.

computationally designed peptide lattices can be controlled by tuning solution conditions.
the design of nanostructures is possible with the careful use of computation and control of solution conditions.
